newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Petaluma warns on merger consequences.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Petaluma warns on merger consequences.

text.p: Petaluma Wines Ltd chairman Brian Croser on Tuesday warned of a downside in recent wine industry takeovers and said the modern corporate culture conspired against long-term value in the industry.

Croser told the premier wine producer's annual meeting that patient investment in research and education by generations of farsighted industry leaders had created the Australian industry's global advantage.

Croser highlighted the current focus on the immediate imperatives of the marketplace, managers using the industry as a success stepping stone, and owners which viewed their investment in the Australian industry as just another component of the global wine trade.
"These are all inevitable features of the modern Australian wine industry, but they do conspire to undermine the investment in the future of our innovative potential," he said.
"Rather, there is a tendency to utilise to the maximum immediate effect the investment of previous generations without a coherent replacement policy," he said.
Croser said there was a downside to the apparent economic rationality of takeovers such as that by Foster's Brewing Group Ltd of Rothbury Wines Ltd and by Southcorp Holdings Ltd of Coldstream Ltd.

"That is the loss of independent, creative growth points in the industry, which have the potential to contribute exponentially to the economic development of the Australian wine industry and the economy of Australia in the future," he said.

Croser said he was comfortable that Petaluma's potential was protected by its financial performance and long-term shareholders "from the premature discharge and dissipation almost inevitable in the takeover of a premium wine company by one of its bigger cousins."
He said the boards and chief executives of Australia's major wine companies must provide leadership in organising research and education, the future key to the industry.
"At the moment the providers are running this agenda in an inefficient fashipn, following their own perceptions of need and achieving their own individual outcomes," he said.
"This in the absence of real industry leadership in the area of investment in the innovative future of the Australian wine industry," Croser said.
